extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, editors, bibliographers, and advanced students of Rabelais/textual criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on producing and assessing editions of Rabelais and on literary-historical judgments about his works (sources, authorship, style, and textual variants). Emphasizes editorial principles, evidence standards for attribution, and methods for tracing sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not amalgamate variant readings
rubrics_metrics.description: A good edition, of course, would make no attempt at amalgamating these. That would give a false impression and end in confusion; but it should note them all, and show them all, not combined, but simply as variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should present all earlier differences as distinct variants rather than combining them into a single 'composite' text; record suppressions and additions and show changes rather than fusing them into one synthesized reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fabricating a text by juxtaposition
rubrics_metrics.description: After Le Duchat, all the editions, in their care that nothing should be lost, made the mistake of collecting and placing side by side things which had no connection with each other, which had even been substituted for each other. The result was a fabricated text, full of contradictions naturally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assemble unconnected or substituted passages side-by-side as if they coexisted in a single authentic version; such practice produces contradictions and a false impression of the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative editorial base: first text with later modifications noted
rubrics_metrics.description: It would also be possible to reverse the method. It would be interesting to take his first text as the basis, noting the later modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may choose the author's earliest printed version as the base text and annotate subsequent insertions/changes to reveal revision processes; this approach can illuminate how the author revised particular passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record authorial revision method (insertions preserved)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rabelais suppressed nothing, modified nothing; he did not change his plan at all. What he did was to make insertions, to slip in between two clauses a new one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing revision history, look for insertions that leave earlier clauses intact rather than wholesale rewrites — these preserve the 'warp' of the earlier clause and reveal the author's method of elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize craftsmanship behind apparent effortlessness
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparison is most instructive, showing us to what an extent Rabelais’ admirable style was due to conscious effort, care, and elaboration... It was modelled and remodelled, repaired, touched up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary analysis should account for conscious revision and craftsmanship (not assume spontaneous perfection); assess evidence of reworking, polishing, and incremental additions as part of stylistic formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit source-claims to what the author could have known
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is of direct interest save what was known to him, what fell under his eyes, what lay to his hand—as the Facetiae of Poggio, and the last sermonnaires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing literary sources, restrict claims to works demonstrably accessible to the author (read or likely to have been read); avoid speculative parallels to materials the author could not plausibly have encountered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require positive traces for claims of antiquity/origin
rubrics_metrics.description: To place such a tradition on a sure basis, positive traces must be forthcoming; and they cannot be adduced even for the most celebrated of these monuments...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertions that characters or names pre-existed the author (e.g., Gargantua as a Celtic/solar myth) demand positive written or testimonial evidence before being accepted; lists of toponyms alone are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify direct classical and contemporary models via textual parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of Aristophanes and of Lucian, his intimate acquaintance with nearly all the writers of antiquity... Pliny especially was his encyclopaedia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish influence by tracing concrete parallels in ideas, phrasing, and topical borrowing (e.g., Pliny for botanical material) rather than by vague resemblance; cite specific passages where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious in attributing works (weigh stylistic and factual evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of the Chronique Gargantuaine is still undecided. Is it by Rabelais or by someone else? Both theories are defensible... it would be dangerous to make too bold an assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribution should balance pros and cons (stylistic quality, points in common, dating) and avoid definitive claims where evidence is equivocal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use printing history and marks of workmanship in authorship judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: First of all, if he had left it complete, would sixteen years have gone by before it was printed? Then, does it bear evident marks of his workmanship? Is the hand of the master visible throughout?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider publication delay, internal evidence of craft, and consistency of 'hand' across the text when assessing whether a work is genuinely by the purported author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate vocabulary novelty and lexical patterns for authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: The fifth book contains from the point of view of the vocabulary really the least novelty. On the contrary, it is full of words and expressions already met with... A very striking point is the profound difference in the use of anatomical terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure authenticity by checking for fresh coinages or characteristic lexical inventions; repetitive reliance on earlier diction or different semantic uses (e.g., anatomical terms used correctly rather than comically) can indicate an imitator or later hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat manuscript quality and paleography as decisive for transcription
rubrics_metrics.description: The writing, extremely flowing and rapid, is execrable, and most difficult to decipher and to transcribe accurately... the writing of a clerk executed as quickly as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the legibility and reliability of manuscript witnesses; transcribe with scrupulous fidelity and note uncertainties rather than emending without justification; poor-quality manuscripts may reflect hurried copying/adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the author's final edition as base text where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: All the editions of Rabelais continue, and rightly, to reproduce the edition of 1564... it is convenient and even necessary to follow and keep to the original edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an authoritative final edition by the author exists, editors should generally adopt it as the base text and present earlier readings as variants unless there are compelling reasons to do otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish clearly authorial core from later additions/adaptations
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sixteen chapters may, and really must be, the text of Rabelais, in the final form as left by him, and the framework, and a number of the passages in the continuation, the best ones, of course, are his, but have been patched up and tampered with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify portions that show the master's hand and treat them as authoritative while marking and critically evaluating later interpolations, adapters' 'improvements', and patched passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious when modernizing orthography
rubrics_metrics.description: He took the trouble first of all to note the spelling of each word. Whenever in a single instance he found it in accordance with modern spelling, he made it the same throughout... Rabelais certainly gained in clearness, but over-zeal is often fatal to a reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document original orthography; any modernization should be conservative and clearly signposted — excessive regularization risks losing historical linguistic features and altering the author's voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor concise, judicious annotation over excessive notes
rubrics_metrics.description: The short footnotes, with all their brevity, contain useful explanations of difficult words... In respect to its precision and the value of its notes, which are short and very judicious, Burgaud des Marets’ edition is valuable... the text is often encumbered by notes which are really too numerous, and, above all, too long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide notes that are precise, relevant, and proportionate; avoid voluminous or speculative annotation that obscures the text or offers imaginary historical explanations without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject historical explanations lacking documentary proof
rubrics_metrics.description: All the historical explanations are purely imaginary, utterly without proof, and should the more emphatically be looked on as baseless and dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotations and critical claims that rest on conjectural historical reconstructions must be grounded in documentary evidence; dismiss fanciful or unsupported historical readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore and present a 'pure and exact' text without retouching
rubrics_metrics.description: It was M. Jannet who in our days first restored the pure and exact text of Rabelais, not only without retouching it, but without making additions or insertions, or juxtaposition of things that were not formerly found together. For each of the books he has followed the last edition issued by Rabelais, and all the earlier differences he gives as variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial policy advocated: follow the author's last issued edition and present earlier variants as such; avoid editorial additions, insertions, or artificial juxtapositions that create a non-authentic 'composite' text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not search for hidden riddles when plain sense suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no mysteries below the surface, and it is a waste of time to look for knots in a bulrush.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive practice should favor straightforward readings supported by textual evidence rather than elaborate hidden-symbol theories; avoid over-interpretation that invents meaning not warranted by the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative literature to trace methods and tone of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Novelle of Gentile Sermini... provided him with the form of the subject, and was the theme for Rabelais’ marvellous variations... Rabelais improves all he borrows, but it is from Folengo he starts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing influence from other national literatures (e.g., Italian burlesque), compare forms, themes, and tones to show how the author adapted and transformed source materials rather than assuming simple copying.
